title: Acute Ascending Cholangitis
subject: Medicine
summary: Acute ascending cholangitis is a bacterial infection of an obstructed biliary tree, classically presenting with Charcot’s triad and often progressing to Reynolds’ pentad. Rapid recognition, resuscitation and biliary drainage are life‑saving.

sections.p: Acute ascending cholangitis is a bacterial infection of a dilated biliary tree, usually secondary to gallstone obstruction. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by laboratory and imaging evidence.
b: Charcot’s triad – fever, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice
Reynolds’ pentad – add hypotension and altered mental status
Elevated bilirubin, ALP, GGT, leukocytosis
Positive blood cultures (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Bacteroides)
Ultrasound shows dilated ducts; CT or MRCP confirms obstruction

t.b: Identify causative organism and guide antibiotic choice – positive in ~70% of cases; a negative culture does not rule out infection
Confirms cholestasis – >2 mg/dL suggests significant obstruction
Elevated in cholestasis – helps differentiate from hepatocellular injury
First imaging – detects ductal dilation and stones; limited in obese or gas-filled patients
Used when ultrasound is inconclusive or to plan ERCP; shows stone location and ductal anatomy

sections.p: Severity is staged by the Tokyo Guidelines 2022, which guide urgency of drainage and antibiotic choice.
b: Grade 1 – mild: no organ dysfunction, stable vitals
Grade 2 – moderate: organ dysfunction (e.g., renal, coagulation) but stable
Grade 3 – severe: shock, organ failure, or altered consciousness

t.b: Assesses organ dysfunction – informs need for intensive care and drainage timing

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, gallstones are the predominant cause, but infections such as HIV, TB, malaria, and herbal hepatotoxins can precipitate or worsen cholangitis.
b: Gallstones obstructing common bile duct
Choledochal cysts
Biliary strictures (post‑surgical or inflammatory)
Infections: HIV (immune compromise), TB (miliary spread), malaria (hepatomegaly)
Herbal remedies causing cholestasis or biliary inflammation

t.b: Rule out viral hepatitis as a concurrent cause of jaundice

sections.p: Patients present with the classic triad, often accompanied by systemic signs of sepsis.
b: High fever with rigors
Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back
Jaundice (icteric sclera, skin)
Hypotension and confusion in severe cases

t.b: Fever >38.5°C, tachycardia, hypotension (<90/60 mmHg) indicates shock

sections.p: Investigations confirm the diagnosis, identify the pathogen, and assess organ dysfunction.

t.b: Leukocytosis with left shift – supports infection
Elevated bilirubin, ALP, GGT – indicates cholestasis
Prolonged PT/INR – guides transfusion and antibiotic timing
Creatinine rise – indicates renal impairment, common in severe cholangitis

sections.p: Early recognition of organ failure and septic shock is critical.
b: Severe sepsis – hypotension, oliguria, altered mentation
Acute liver failure – INR >1.5, encephalopathy
Biliary peritonitis – peritoneal signs, free air on imaging

sections.p: Immediate resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage are the pillars of treatment.
b: Resuscitate with crystalloids and oxygen
Broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics – piperacillin‑tazobactam or 3rd‑gen cephalosporin + metronidazole; avoid fluoroquinolones in renal impairment
Correct coagulopathy – vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma if INR >1.5
Urgent ERCP within 24–72 hrs for stone removal or stenting
Consider percutaneous drainage if ERCP fails or is unavailable

t.b: Piperacillin‑tazobactam covers gram‑negative rods and anaerobes; alternatives if unavailable
Within 24–72 hrs reduces mortality; earlier if shock

sections.p: Monitor liver function, renal status and repeat imaging; counsel on stone prevention and safe herbal use.
b: Repeat LFTs and bilirubin every 48 hrs until normal
Ultrasound 1–2 weeks post‑ERCP to confirm ductal clearance
Educate on low‑fat diet, weight control, and avoiding hepatotoxic herbs

t.b: Ensures no residual stones or ductal dilation

sections.p: Other causes of jaundice and RUQ pain can mimic cholangitis.
b: Acute hepatitis – no RUQ pain, no fever
Choledocholithiasis without infection – no fever, no leukocytosis
Acute pancreatitis – epigastric pain, lipase elevation

t.b: Elevated in pancreatitis, normal in cholangitis

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal in low‑resource settings.
b: Leukocytosis may be blunted in HIV; consider culture even if WBC normal
Bilirubin may be normal early; repeat if high suspicion
Ultrasound may miss stones in obese patients; use CT if available

faq.a: Fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice – classic presentation of ascending cholangitis.
It removes the obstruction, stops bacterial spread and reduces mortality.
No – intravenous broad‑spectrum antibiotics are required until the infection is controlled.

exam: 1. A 55‑year‑old presents with fever, RUQ pain and jaundice. Blood cultures grow E. coli. What is the next step? — Urgent ERCP within 24–72 hrs to relieve obstruction and prevent sepsis.

2. A patient with cholangitis develops hypotension and confusion. What is the most appropriate immediate management? — Resuscitate with crystalloids, give IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and start vasopressors if needed.
3. Which laboratory value best indicates cholestasis? — Elevated bilirubin >2 mg/dL and ALP/GGT rise.
4. A patient with gallstone cholangitis is allergic to penicillin. What antibiotic regimen is acceptable? — Third‑generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole.

5. How do you differentiate cholangitis from acute pancreatitis on bedside exam? — Pancreatitis has epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase; cholangitis has RUQ pain, jaundice and fever.
6. What is Reynolds’ pentad and why is it significant? — Charcot’s triad plus hypotension and altered mental status; indicates severe sepsis and requires immediate intervention.
7. In a setting without ERCP, what alternative drainage can be used? — Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage.
8. Why is vitamin K given in cholangitis? — To correct coagulopathy from impaired hepatic synthesis and reduce bleeding risk before invasive procedures.
